Shor's Discrete Logarithm Algorithm¶

Recover a discrete logarithm by sampling the Fourier transform of a hidden subgroup of Zr×Zr\mathbb{Z}_r\times\mathbb{Z}_rZr​×Zr​, then combining the resulting congruences with the extended Euclidean algorithm.

The problem · Quantum section · Classical section · Success and cost

The notebook includes executable Qiskit circuits, classical recovery for composite group orders, and a rendered record of the results. Run the cells from top to bottom. All quantum computations use a local ideal simulator.

1. The problem¶

Let C=⟨g⟩C=\langle g\rangleC=⟨g⟩ be a cyclic group of known order rrr. Given h∈Ch\in Ch∈C, find the unique exponent a∈{0,…,r−1}a\in\{0,\ldots,r-1\}a∈{0,…,r−1} satisfying

h=ga.h=g^a.h=ga.

The group operation and equality of group elements are assumed to be efficiently computable. The order rrr is part of the input and need not be prime. Computing the order, when it is unknown, is a separate task.

For the concrete implementation, ppp is a prime and CCC is the subgroup generated by ggg in the multiplicative group modulo ppp. Thus

ga≡h(modp),r=ord⁡p(g),r∣p−1.g^a\equiv h\pmod p, \qquad r=\operatorname{ord}_p(g), \qquad r\mid p-1.ga≡h(modp),r=ordp​(g),r∣p−1.

The exponent modulus rrr and the residue modulus ppp have different roles. The two quantum input registers represent exponents modulo rrr, while the output register represents residues modulo ppp.

We use the known-order hidden subgroup formulation of Shor's discrete logarithm algorithm. The code assumes the promises that ppp is prime, ggg has exact order rrr, and h∈⟨g⟩h\in\langle g\rangleh∈⟨g⟩. Its basic parameter checks do not prove primality or certify the exact order. The examples use explicitly known groups. For r=1r=1r=1, the only discrete logarithm is zero. The circuits below treat r≥2r\geq2r≥2.

The hidden subgroup¶

Set G=Zr×ZrG=\mathbb{Z}_r\times\mathbb{Z}_rG=Zr​×Zr​ and define

f(x,y)=gxh−y=gx−ay.f(x,y)=g^xh^{-y}=g^{x-ay}.f(x,y)=gxh−y=gx−ay.

This function can be evaluated using the known elements ggg and hhh. Constructing it does not require the unknown exponent aaa.

Since ggg has exact order rrr,

f(x,y)=f(x′,y′)⟺x−x′≡a(y−y′)(modr)⟺(x−x′,y−y′)∈K,\begin{aligned} f(x,y)=f(x',y') &\Longleftrightarrow x-x'\equiv a(y-y')\pmod r\\ &\Longleftrightarrow (x-x',y-y')\in K, \end{aligned}f(x,y)=f(x′,y′)​⟺x−x′≡a(y−y′)(modr)⟺(x−x′,y−y′)∈K,​

where

K={(at,t):t∈Zr}=⟨(a,1)⟩.K=\{(at,t):t\in\mathbb{Z}_r\}=\langle(a,1)\rangle.K={(at,t):t∈Zr​}=⟨(a,1)⟩.

Thus fff is constant on each coset of KKK and separates different cosets. The subgroup has rrr elements. It records the unknown logarithm in the relation between its two coordinates. The group CCC contains the function values, while GGG is the domain of the hidden subgroup problem.

2. Quantum section¶

Create a coset state¶

Prepare both exponent registers uniformly and evaluate the function in a third register:

1r∑x,y=0r−1∣x,y⟩∣1⟩⟼1r∑x,y=0r−1∣x,y⟩∣gxh−y⟩.\frac1r\sum_{x,y=0}^{r-1}\lvert x,y\rangle\lvert1\rangle \longmapsto \frac1r\sum_{x,y=0}^{r-1}\lvert x,y\rangle\lvert g^xh^{-y}\rangle.r1​x,y=0∑r−1​∣x,y⟩∣1⟩⟼r1​x,y=0∑r−1​∣x,y⟩∣gxh−y⟩.

Here ∣1⟩\lvert1\rangle∣1⟩ encodes the multiplicative identity. The implementation uses controlled modular multiplications on the output register.

To analyze the state, imagine measuring the output and obtaining f(x0,y0)f(x_0,y_0)f(x0​,y0​). The first two registers are then in the normalized coset state

∣(x0,y0)+K⟩=1r∑t=0r−1∣x0+at, y0+t⟩,\lvert(x_0,y_0)+K\rangle =\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_{t=0}^{r-1} \lvert x_0+at,\ y_0+t\rangle,∣(x0​,y0​)+K⟩=r​1​t=0∑r−1​∣x0​+at, y0​+t⟩,

with both coordinates taken modulo rrr.

The circuit does not measure the output register. Ignoring it gives the same measurement statistics on the exponent registers as measuring it and discarding the outcome.

Fourier sampling reveals a linear congruence¶

Let ωr=e2πi/r\omega_r=e^{2\pi i/r}ωr​=e2πi/r and use the positive-exponent transform

Fr∣x⟩=1r∑u=0r−1ωrxu∣u⟩.F_r\lvert x\rangle =\frac1{\sqrt r}\sum_{u=0}^{r-1}\omega_r^{xu}\lvert u\rangle.Fr​∣x⟩=r​1​u=0∑r−1​ωrxu​∣u⟩.

Applying FrF_rFr​ to each coordinate of the coset state gives

(Fr⊗Fr)∣(x0,y0)+K⟩=1rr∑u,v=0r−1ωrx0u+y0v(∑t=0r−1ωrt(au+v))∣u,v⟩.(F_r\otimes F_r)\lvert(x_0,y_0)+K\rangle =\frac1{r\sqrt r} \sum_{u,v=0}^{r-1} \omega_r^{x_0u+y_0v} \left(\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}\omega_r^{t(au+v)}\right) \lvert u,v\rangle.(Fr​⊗Fr​)∣(x0​,y0​)+K⟩=rr​1​u,v=0∑r−1​ωrx0​u+y0​v​(t=0∑r−1​ωrt(au+v)​)∣u,v⟩.

The inner geometric sum is rrr when au+v≡0(modr)au+v\equiv0\pmod rau+v≡0(modr) and zero otherwise. Therefore the measurement distribution is

Pr⁡(U=u,V=v)={1/r,au+v≡0(modr),0,otherwise.\Pr(U=u,V=v)= \begin{cases} 1/r,&au+v\equiv0\pmod r,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases}Pr(U=u,V=v)={1/r,0,​au+v≡0(modr),otherwise.​

Each shot gives a uniformly random u∈Zru\in\mathbb{Z}_ru∈Zr​ together with

v≡−au(modr).v\equiv-au\pmod r.v≡−au(modr).

Equivalently, the measured pair belongs to the annihilator

K⊥={(u,v)∈Zr2:au+v≡0(modr)}.K^\perp=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb{Z}_r^2:au+v\equiv0\pmod r\}.K⊥={(u,v)∈Zr2​:au+v≡0(modr)}.

The minus sign follows from our choice f(x,y)=gxh−yf(x,y)=g^xh^{-y}f(x,y)=gxh−y. It must be preserved in the classical recovery code.

Qubit registers and Fourier transforms¶

Let n=⌈log⁡2r⌉n=\lceil\log_2r\rceiln=⌈log2​r⌉ and m=⌈log⁡2p⌉m=\lceil\log_2p\rceilm=⌈log2​p⌉. The circuit uses two nnn-qubit exponent registers and one mmm-qubit output register.

For r=2nr=2^nr=2n, Qiskit's QFTGate implements FrF_rFr​. Initial uniform states are prepared with Hadamard gates.

For other rrr, use the extension

F~r=Fr⊕I2n−r.\widetilde F_r=F_r\oplus I_{2^n-r}.Fr​=Fr​⊕I2n−r​.

Applying it to zero prepares a uniform superposition over exactly the valid exponents 0,…,r−10,\ldots,r-10,…,r−1. A second application after the oracle performs Fourier sampling. An ordinary nnn-qubit QFT would instead transform modulo 2n2^n2n and would not give the exact congruences derived above.

The non-power-of-two transform is stored as a dense UnitaryGate. It represents the mathematical transform to floating-point precision. This choice makes small examples transparent, but its O(r2)O(r^2)O(r2) matrix storage is not a scalable implementation in log⁡r\log rlogr.

In [3]:
def exponent_width(r):
    if not isinstance(r, int) or r < 2:
        raise ValueError("The known order r must be an integer at least 2.")
    return (r - 1).bit_length()


def finite_qft(r):
    '''Positive-exponent F_r with identity on unused basis states.'''
    n = exponent_width(r)
    dimension = 1 << n
    if r == dimension:
        gate = QFTGate(n)
        gate.label = rf"$F_{{{r}}}$"
        return gate
    indices = np.arange(r)
    block = np.exp(2j * np.pi * np.outer(indices, indices) / r) / np.sqrt(r)
    matrix = np.eye(dimension, dtype=complex)
    matrix[:r, :r] = block
    return UnitaryGate(matrix, label=rf"$F_{{{r}}}$")


def check_parameters(p, g, h, r):
    '''Basic checks. Primality and exact generator order remain promises.'''
    n = exponent_width(r)
    if not isinstance(p, int) or p < 3 or (p - 1) % r:
        raise ValueError("Require p >= 3 and r dividing p - 1.")
    if (not isinstance(g, int) or not isinstance(h, int)
            or not 1 <= g < p or not 1 <= h < p):
        raise ValueError("g and h must be nonzero residues modulo p.")
    if gcd(g, p) != 1 or gcd(h, p) != 1:
        raise ValueError("g and h must be invertible modulo p.")
    if pow(g, r, p) != 1 or pow(h, r, p) != 1:
        raise ValueError("The elements are inconsistent with the supplied order.")
    return n, (p - 1).bit_length()

Implement the function with modular multipliers¶

For an invertible residue ccc, define a gate McM_cMc​ by

Mc∣z⟩={∣cz mod p⟩,0≤z<p,∣z⟩,p≤z<2m.M_c\lvert z\rangle= \begin{cases} \lvert cz\bmod p\rangle,&0\leq z<p,\\ \lvert z\rangle,&p\leq z<2^m. \end{cases}Mc​∣z⟩={∣czmodp⟩,∣z⟩,​0≤z<p,p≤z<2m.​

Multiplication by ccc permutes the valid residues, and the unused encodings are fixed, so this is unitary.

Write the input integers in binary. For each set bit of xxx, multiply the output by the corresponding power g2jg^{2^j}g2j. For each set bit of yyy, multiply it by h−2jh^{-2^j}h−2j. Starting at 111 gives gxh−yg^xh^{-y}gxh−y. The inverse of hhh is computable from the public residue and does not require its discrete logarithm.

The following builder uses controlled permutation matrices for these multipliers. It never searches for aaa or constructs a table indexed by possible logarithms. The matrices are nevertheless large for large ppp. They serve as explicit small-instance arithmetic gates.

In [4]:
def modular_multiplier(c, p):
    '''Multiply valid residues by c, fixing unused output encodings.'''
    if not isinstance(p, int) or p < 3:
        raise ValueError("p must be an integer at least 3.")
    if not isinstance(c, int) or gcd(c, p) != 1:
        raise ValueError("The multiplier must be invertible modulo p.")
    c %= p
    m = (p - 1).bit_length()
    dimension = 1 << m
    matrix = np.zeros((dimension, dimension), dtype=complex)
    for z in range(dimension):
        target = (c * z) % p if z < p else z
        matrix[target, z] = 1
    return UnitaryGate(matrix, label=f"M_{c}")


def make_dlog_oracle(p, g, h, r):
    '''Controlled multiplications evaluate g**x * h**(-y) modulo p.'''
    n, m = check_parameters(p, g, h, r)
    circuit = QuantumCircuit(2 * n + m, name="U_gh")
    output = list(range(2 * n, 2 * n + m))
    g_power = g
    inverse_h_power = pow(h, -1, p)
    for bit in range(n):
        if g_power != 1:
            circuit.append(
                modular_multiplier(g_power, p).control(1),
                [bit] + output,
            )
        if inverse_h_power != 1:
            circuit.append(
                modular_multiplier(inverse_h_power, p).control(1),
                [n + bit] + output,
            )
        g_power = (g_power * g_power) % p
        inverse_h_power = (inverse_h_power * inverse_h_power) % p
    return circuit.to_gate(label=r"$U_{g,h}$")

Sample both exponent registers¶

The circuit below prepares the output register at 111, queries the multiplication oracle, and measures the two transformed exponent registers.

Qiskit qubit 000 is the least significant bit, so each measurement string is converted directly to an integer. Keep the two results from the same shot together. Independently combining the marginal counts would lose the correlation v≡−au(modr)v\equiv-au\pmod rv≡−au(modr).

The sampler uses a persistent random generator. Repeated batches therefore advance the random state.

In [5]:
def dlog_sampling_circuit(oracle, r, p):
    n = exponent_width(r)
    if not isinstance(p, int) or p < 3:
        raise ValueError("p must be an integer at least 3.")
    m = (p - 1).bit_length()
    if oracle.num_qubits != 2 * n + m:
        raise ValueError("The oracle size does not match the three registers.")

    x = QuantumRegister(n, "x")
    y = QuantumRegister(n, "y")
    z = QuantumRegister(m, "z")
    u = ClassicalRegister(n, "u")
    v = ClassicalRegister(n, "v")
    circuit = QuantumCircuit(x, y, z, u, v)
    fourier = finite_qft(r)
    for register in (x, y):
        if r == 1 << n:
            circuit.h(register)
        else:
            circuit.append(fourier, list(register))
    circuit.x(z[0])
    circuit.append(oracle, list(x) + list(y) + list(z))
    circuit.append(fourier, list(x))
    circuit.append(fourier, list(y))
    circuit.measure(x, u)
    circuit.measure(y, v)
    return circuit


def sample_dlog_pairs(oracle, r, p, shots, sampler):
    if not isinstance(shots, int) or shots < 1:
        raise ValueError("shots must be a positive integer.")
    circuit = dlog_sampling_circuit(oracle, r, p)
    result = sampler.run([circuit], shots=shots).result()[0]
    u_bits = result.data.u.get_bitstrings()
    v_bits = result.data.v.get_bitstrings()
    pairs = [
        (int(u, 2), int(v, 2))
        for u, v in zip(u_bits, v_bits, strict=True)
    ]
    if any(u >= r or v >= r for u, v in pairs):
        raise RuntimeError("An unused exponent encoding was measured.")
    return pairs

3. Classical section¶

Combine samples when the group order is composite¶

Each sample satisfies

aui≡−vi(modr).au_i\equiv-v_i\pmod r.aui​≡−vi​(modr).

If gcd⁡(ui,r)=1\gcd(u_i,r)=1gcd(ui​,r)=1, then a≡−viui−1(modr)a\equiv-v_i u_i^{-1}\pmod ra≡−vi​ui−1​(modr). For composite rrr, a nonzero uiu_iui​ need not have an inverse. Discarding all such samples would throw away useful information.

Instead, put

d=gcd⁡(r,u1,…,ut).d=\gcd(r,u_1,\ldots,u_t).d=gcd(r,u1​,…,ut​).

When d=1d=1d=1, the extended Euclidean algorithm gives integers c0,c1,…,ctc_0,c_1,\ldots,c_tc0​,c1​,…,ct​ such that

c0r+∑i=1tciui=1.c_0r+\sum_{i=1}^t c_i u_i=1.c0​r+i=1∑t​ci​ui​=1.

Multiply by aaa and substitute the sampled congruences:

a≡∑i=1tciaui≡−∑i=1tcivi(modr).a\equiv\sum_{i=1}^t c_i a u_i \equiv-\sum_{i=1}^t c_i v_i\pmod r.a≡i=1∑t​ci​aui​≡−i=1∑t​ci​vi​(modr).

Thus several samples can recover aaa even when none of their first coordinates is individually invertible modulo rrr. For example, the coefficients 222 and 333 together generate 111 modulo 666.

Implement the extended Euclidean update¶

The code maintains integers ddd and bbb satisfying

d=gcd⁡(r,u1,…,ut),da≡b(modr).d=\gcd(r,u_1,\ldots,u_t), \qquad da\equiv b\pmod r.d=gcd(r,u1​,…,ut​),da≡b(modr).

Initially, d=rd=rd=r and b=0b=0b=0. For a new pair (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), compute integers α,β\alpha,\betaα,β with

d′=gcd⁡(d,u)=αd+βu.d'=\gcd(d,u)=\alpha d+\beta u.d′=gcd(d,u)=αd+βu.

The updated relation follows directly:

d′a≡αb−βv(modr).d'a\equiv\alpha b-\beta v\pmod r.d′a≡αb−βv(modr).

Set b′=(αb−βv) mod rb'=(\alpha b-\beta v)\bmod rb′=(αb−βv)modr. When d′=1d'=1d′=1, the logarithm is a=b′a=b'a=b′. The reduction of b′b'b′ modulo rrr keeps the stored integers small.

For consistent ideal samples, if d>1d>1d>1, then ddd divides bbb and the relation determines aaa only modulo r/dr/dr/d. There remain ddd possible residues modulo rrr. This implementation waits for more information instead of searching those candidates.

In [8]:
def extended_gcd(a, b):
    '''Return d, alpha, beta with alpha*a + beta*b = d = gcd(a, b).'''
    if (not isinstance(a, int) or not isinstance(b, int)
            or a < 0 or b < 0):
        raise ValueError("The Euclidean inputs must be nonnegative integers.")
    old_r, remainder = a, b
    old_s, s = 1, 0
    old_t, t = 0, 1
    while remainder:
        quotient = old_r // remainder
        old_r, remainder = remainder, old_r - quotient * remainder
        old_s, s = s, old_s - quotient * s
        old_t, t = t, old_t - quotient * t
    return old_r, old_s, old_t


def update_log_constraint(r, d, b, pairs):
    '''Update d*a = b (mod r) using the measured pair constraints.'''
    exponent_width(r)
    if not isinstance(d, int) or d < 1 or r % d:
        raise ValueError("d must be a positive divisor of r.")
    if not isinstance(b, int) or not 0 <= b < r:
        raise ValueError("b must be an integer in [0, r).")
    for pair in pairs:
        if not isinstance(pair, (tuple, list)) or len(pair) != 2:
            raise ValueError("Each sample must be an (u, v) pair.")
        u, v = pair
        if (not isinstance(u, int) or not isinstance(v, int)
                or not 0 <= u < r or not 0 <= v < r):
            raise ValueError("The sample coordinates must be in [0, r).")
        new_d, alpha, beta = extended_gcd(d, u)
        b = (alpha * b - beta * v) % r
        d = new_d
    return d, b


def logarithm_candidate(r, pairs):
    d, b = update_log_constraint(r, r, 0, pairs)
    return (b if d == 1 else None), d

Verify the result and bound the sampling loop¶

When the combined gcd reaches 111, verify the candidate with the original discrete logarithm equation:

ga mod p=h.g^a\bmod p=h.gamodp=h.

Because ggg has exact order rrr, at most one candidate in {0,…,r−1}\{0,\ldots,r-1\}{0,…,r−1} passes. A failed check is reported as an error, rather than returning an unverified answer.

If the gcd is still larger than 111, collect another batch of quantum samples. A fixed batch limit prevents an indefinite loop. The state (d,b)(d,b)(d,b) is updated incrementally, so earlier samples need not be stored.

For h=1h=1h=1, the unique logarithm in the chosen range is 000. That case can be answered directly without quantum sampling.

In [10]:
def recover_discrete_log(
    oracle, p, g, h, r, *, batch_size=6, max_batches=6, seed=2026
):
    '''Recover and verify a in [0, r), without supplying a to the solver.'''
    n, m = check_parameters(p, g, h, r)
    if oracle.num_qubits != 2 * n + m:
        raise ValueError("The oracle size is inconsistent with the parameters.")
    if (not isinstance(batch_size, int) or batch_size < 1
            or not isinstance(max_batches, int) or max_batches < 1):
        raise ValueError("Batch size and maximum batches must be positive.")
    if h == 1:
        return {"logarithm": 0, "sample_count": 0, "batches": 0,
                "verified": True}

    sampler = StatevectorSampler(seed=np.random.default_rng(seed))
    d, b = r, 0
    sample_count = 0
    for batch in range(1, max_batches + 1):
        new_pairs = sample_dlog_pairs(oracle, r, p, batch_size, sampler)
        sample_count += len(new_pairs)
        d, b = update_log_constraint(r, d, b, new_pairs)
        if d == 1:
            if pow(g, b, p) != h:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    "The candidate failed g**a mod p == h. "
                    "Check the oracle, group promises, and sample quality."
                )
            return {"logarithm": b, "sample_count": sample_count,
                    "batches": batch, "verified": True}
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"The combined gcd is {d} after {sample_count} samples. "
        "Increase max_batches for another bounded attempt."
    )

Run the complete algorithm¶

This call receives the public instance (p,g,h,r)(p,g,h,r)(p,g,h,r) and its oracle. The unknown logarithm is not used in the circuit construction or supplied to the recovery routine.

Insufficient samples and other group orders¶

The sample (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) supplies no information. For r=6r=6r=6, the pair (2,4)(2,4)(2,4) alone also leaves the logarithm undetermined, because its first coordinate shares a factor with rrr.

The remaining examples include the zero logarithm, a prime-order subgroup, a group whose order is a power of two, and the logarithm r−1r-1r−1.

In [12]:
for partial in [[], [(0, 0)], [(2, 4)]]:
    candidate, divisor = logarithm_candidate(6, partial)
    assert candidate is None
    print(f"Samples {partial}: gcd={divisor}, more samples are needed.")

cases = [
    ("Zero logarithm", 7, 3, 6, 1, 0),
    ("Prime-order subgroup", 7, 2, 3, 4, 2),
    ("Power-of-two order", 5, 2, 4, 3, 3),
    ("Logarithm r-1", 7, 3, 6, 5, 5),
]
for label, prime, generator, order, target, expected in cases:
    test_oracle = make_dlog_oracle(prime, generator, target, order)
    recovered = recover_discrete_log(
        test_oracle, prime, generator, target, order, seed=41
    )
    assert recovered["logarithm"] == expected
    print(f"{label}: a={recovered['logarithm']}, shots={recovered['sample_count']}")

4. Success probability and computational cost¶

The first coordinate uuu of each ideal sample is uniform modulo rrr. After t≥1t\geq1t≥1 independent shots, insufficient information means

gcd⁡(r,u1,…,ut)>1.\gcd(r,u_1,\ldots,u_t)>1.gcd(r,u1​,…,ut​)>1.

Then some prime divisor ℓ\ellℓ of rrr divides every uiu_iui​, an event of probability ℓ−t\ell^{-t}ℓ−t. Hence

Pr⁡(insufficient information)≤∑ℓ∣r, ℓ primeℓ−t≤ω(r)2−t≤n2−t,\Pr(\text{insufficient information}) \leq\sum_{\ell\mid r,\ \ell\ {\rm prime}}\ell^{-t} \leq\omega(r)2^{-t} \leq n2^{-t},Pr(insufficient information)≤ℓ∣r, ℓ prime∑​ℓ−t≤ω(r)2−t≤n2−t,

where ω(r)\omega(r)ω(r) counts distinct prime factors and n=⌈log⁡2r⌉n=\lceil\log_2r\rceiln=⌈log2​r⌉. Thus t≥⌈log⁡2(n/δ)⌉t\geq\lceil\log_2(n/\delta)\rceilt≥⌈log2​(n/δ)⌉ suffices for failure probability at most δ\deltaδ, with 0<δ<10<\delta<10<δ<1. No factorization of rrr is needed by the recovery algorithm.

The sampling loop returns a verified logarithm or reports failure. Its exact-distribution analysis assumes the promised group and ideal Fourier transforms. It does not model hardware noise.

Let CF(r)C_F(r)CF​(r) be the gate cost of one Fourier transform on an exponent register and CM(p)C_M(p)CM​(p) the cost of one controlled multiplication by a known residue modulo ppp. The oracle uses at most 2n2n2n such multiplications. For ttt samples, a sufficient quantum gate and measurement bound is

O ⁣(t(4CF(r)+2nCM(p)+n+m)),m=⌈log⁡2p⌉.O\!\left(t\left(4C_F(r)+2nC_M(p)+n+m\right)\right), \qquad m=\lceil\log_2p\rceil.O(t(4CF​(r)+2nCM​(p)+n+m)),m=⌈log2​p⌉.

When r=2nr=2^nr=2n, the exact QFT uses O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) Hadamard and controlled-phase gates in a model allowing the required rotation angles. The two initial uniform states then need only 2n2n2n Hadamard gates. For other orders, the dense Fourier matrices here use O(r2)O(r^2)O(r2) entries. Each explicit modular-multiplication matrix uses O(p2)O(p^2)O(p2) entries. These matrices make the small circuits executable, but they do not realize the scalable arithmetic and Fourier constructions needed for Shor's polynomial-time complexity.

The classical recovery stores only ddd and bbb plus the current batch. Their sizes are O(n)O(n)O(n) bits. An extended Euclidean computation takes O(n)O(n)O(n) iterations on these inputs. Charging a conservative O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) schoolbook bit cost per iteration gives O(tn3)O(tn^3)O(tn3) bit operations for the updates. A batch of sss pairs occupies O(sn)O(sn)O(sn) bits. Verifying the final candidate by repeated squaring takes O(n)O(n)O(n) modular multiplications on mmm-bit integers, or a sufficient O(nm2)O(nm^2)O(nm2) schoolbook bit bound.

The controlled multipliers use repeated squaring of public constants. Their classical construction never solves a discrete logarithm. However, retaining up to 2n2n2n dense multiplication matrices can require O(np2)O(np^2)O(np2) complex entries. Statevector simulation separately uses O(22n+m)O(2^{2n+m})O(22n+m) complex amplitudes. Keep the demonstrated group sizes small.
